content: Carbon-containing compounds are extraordinarily numerous, with estimates suggesting there are nearly ten million distinct compounds known to contain carbon atoms. However, the actual number may be even higher. Every organic compound contains at least one carbon atom. The number of these organic compounds is vast, likely approaching ten million. Inorganic carbon chemistry encompasses a wide variety of compounds that do not fall under the domain of organic chemistry. Among the most well-known inorganic carbon compounds are the oxides of carbon, such as carbon dioxide (CO₂) and carbon monoxide (CO). Other less common oxides include carbon suboxide (C₃O₂), dicarbon monoxide (C₂O), and the exotic carbon trioxide (CO₃). The only known acid derived from these oxides is carbonic acid (H₂CO₃). When carbonic acid undergoes monodeprotonation, bicarbonates are formed, which can further deprotonate to yield carbonates. Other types of inorganic carbon compounds include inorganic salts and complexes of carbon-containing polyatomic ions, such as cyanide, isocyanide, cyanate, thiocyanate, and carbide. Metal carbonyls are another class of inorganic carbon compounds, consisting of complexes formed with the neutral ligand CO. The inorganic chemistry of carbon allotropes, such as diamond, graphite, and fullerenes, has significantly advanced since the discovery of buckminsterfullerene in 1985. This discovery led to the identification of additional fullerenes and their derivatives. One notable class of derivatives is inclusion compounds, where an ion is encapsulated within the all-carbon shell of a fullerene. This inclusion is denoted using the @ symbol. For example, a lithium ion trapped within buckminsterfullerene is represented as Li⁺@C₆₀. Like other ionic compounds, this complex ion can pair with a counterion to form a salt. For a more comprehensive listing of inorganic carbon compounds, refer to the Wikipedia page Inorganic compounds by element: Carbon. Several alloys also contain carbon, with carbon steel being the most well-known example. Other iron-carbon alloys include anthracite iron, cast iron, pig iron, and wrought iron. Additionally, spiegel iron (which also contains manganese) is another example. Stellite is an alloy of carbon with cobalt, chromium, and tungsten.
